column2: To forgo present pleasure when the time is at hand and to hope for pleasure yet to come is not the way of the wise.
He who makes an alliance with an enemy and sleeps happily, trusting, is like one asleep at the top of a tree, who wakes only when fallen.
By whatever deed, mild or harsh, one should lift up one's distressed self here; when able, one should practise dharma.
Those who are rivals of his rivals he should draw to himself; and he should know the spies placed by others against himself.
Spies should be well posted, for himself and against the other; he should send heretics, ascetics and the like into the enemy's realm.
In gardens, pleasure-grounds, drinking-halls, lodgings, taverns, brothels, holy places and assemblies,
sinful spies who feign dharma are thorns of the world and gather there; knowing them, he should restrain them and even pacify them.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor even trust the trusted; fear follows the trusting; one should not trust without testing.
Having made the other trust, by a reason that is real, one should strike at him in time when his foot has slipped a little.
One should suspect even what is beyond suspicion, and ever suspect the suspected; for fear born of suspicion cuts even the root.
With attentiveness, silence, ochre robes, matted locks and deerskins, having made a hater trust you, you should pounce on him as a wolf does.
Whether son, brother, father or friend, those who obstruct one's purpose, though they increase one's prosperity, are to be slain.
Even a teacher who is puffed up, who does not know what should and should not be done, and who has taken the wrong path, is properly ruled by the rod.
By rising to greet and saluting, by giving, one may become the slayer of someone's abundance, like a bird with a sharp beak.
Without cutting the vital parts of others, without doing a dreadful deed, without killing, like a fisherman, one does not gain supreme fortune.
By birth there is no such thing as an enemy, and no friend exists; friends and enemies are born from the conjunction of capability.
He should never release an enemy, even one who speaks piteously; he should not cause him pain there, but should slay one who has done harm before.
Effort should always be made, without envy, in gathering and favouring; and restraint too should be practised with effort by one desiring prosperity.
About to strike, one should speak pleasantly; having struck, one should speak more pleasantly still; having cut off his head, one may weep or even grieve.
One should invite with conciliation, honour and patience; hope is the cause; this is what one desiring prosperity should do.
One should not make dry enmity, nor cross a river with one's arms; chewing a cow's horn is useless and shortens life: the teeth are worn and no juice is obtained.
In the three aims of life there are three kinds of affliction and three consequences; knowing the consequence and the killing, one should avoid affliction.
A remaining debt, a remaining fire and a remaining enemy grow again and again, even if small, when not checked.
A debt that grows and enemies that are scorned bring severe misfortune, as do diseases that are neglected.
One should not be one who acts improperly; he should always be watchful; even a thorn badly removed causes trouble for long.
By the killing of men, by fouling the roads, and by the destruction of mines, one should ruin an enemy's realm.
With the sight of a vulture, the stillness of a heron, the doings of a dog and the prowess of a lion, unagitated, wary like a crow, he should act as a serpent acts.
He should guard his ministers against the secret overtures of the heads of guilds, against the appeals of favourites, and against division and combination.
He is mild, they despise him; "he is sharp," they are alarmed; let him be sharp at the time for sharpness, and mild at the time for mildness.
With mildness one kills the very mild, with mildness one kills the dreadful; nothing is impossible by mildness; therefore mildness is the sharper.
He who is mild in season and dreadful in season accomplishes his tasks and stands over his enemies.
One at enmity with a wise man should not trust, thinking "I am far away"; the arms of the intelligent are long, with which, when harmed, he harms.
One should not cross what one cannot reach the far shore of, nor take what the other would take back, nor dig what one cannot dig up the root of, nor slay him whose head one cannot bring down.
Thus has been said what is bound up with crooked conduct; a man should not act in this way; but how could he not hear what is applied by others? Hence it was told by me, wishing your good.'
Having heard the words, beneficial and duly spoken, from the brahmana, the king of the Sauviras acted accordingly, with an undismayed mind, and enjoyed blazing fortune with his kinsmen."
[Yudhishthira said:] "When the limits are broken down, the settled determination of dharma disturbed, and the world oppressed by kings or by thieves, lord of the people,
when all the stages of life are bewildered and rites are spoiled, and people see fear from desire, delusion and greed, Bharata,
when all are distrustful and ever afraid, being slain by deceit and cheating one another,
when regions are ablaze, brahminhood is oppressed, the rain does not fall, and mutual division has arisen,
when the whole livelihood of the earth has fallen to robbers, by what may a brahmana live when a base time has come,
not wishing to abandon his sons and grandsons out of compassion, lord of men? How should he conduct himself in calamity? Tell me that, grandsire.
And how should a king conduct himself when the world has fallen into corruption? How would he not fall from wealth and from dharma, scourge of foes?"
[Bhishma said:] "Security and welfare and good rain have the king as their root, great king; and in the subjects, diseases, death and fears likewise.
When such a time arrives that brings fault upon the people, then one must live by relying on the strength of knowledge.
Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Vishvamitra with a chandala in a village of outcastes.
Long ago, at the junction of the Treta and Dvapara ages, by the course of divine ordinance, a terrible drought of twelve years came about, king.
When the subjects had greatly multiplied, at the approach of the end of the age, at the close of the Treta and the onset of the Dvapara,
the thousand-eyed Indra did not rain; Jupiter turned retrograde; the moon, its mark reversed, went to the southern path.
There was no dew even at night's end, how then rows of clouds; the rivers, their floods of water shrunk, vanished somewhere within.
Lakes, rivers, wells and springs were seen robbed of their lustre, by a nature caused by fate.
The water-stands dried up, the assemblies and drinking-booths ceased, sacrifice and study stopped, and the vashat call and auspicious rites were gone.
Farming and cow-keeping were ruined, markets and shops closed, guild agreements ended, and great festivals perished.
Strewn with bones and skeletons, filled with people crying "alas," with cities mostly empty and villages burnt out,
by thieves in some places, by weapons in others, by afflicted kings elsewhere, and from fear of one another, the land was mostly empty and deserted.
The thoughts of the gods were gone, old and young were lost, cattle, sheep and buffaloes were gone, and people robbed one another.
Brahmanas slain, protection slain, stores of herbs destroyed, the earth then became mostly filled with pale human forms.
In that terrifying time, with dharma failing, Yudhishthira, hungry mortals wandered, eating one another.
Sages abandoned their vows, forsook the fires and gods, left their hermitages, and ran about here and there.
Then the blessed great sage Vishvamitra, homeless, seized by hunger, the wise one, ran about on every side.
Once, as he wandered, he came upon a settlement of dog-eaters, cruel killers of living things, somewhere in the forest.
It was strewn with broken pots, covered with dog-skins, crowded with the bones of boars and asses and with skulls and jars,
spread with the clothes of the dead, with ornaments made from offerings, its huts and cells marked with garlands of snakes' slough,
surrounded by shrines with owl-feather banners, furnished with iron bells, and encircled by packs of dogs.
Entering it, seized by hunger, the great sage, the son of Gadhi, engaged in searching for food, made the greatest effort.
Though begging, Kaushika found nothing anywhere there: no meat, no grain, no roots or fruit, nor anything else.
Alas, I have met with hardship, Kaushika determined, and from weakness fell to the ground in that outcaste village.
The sage thought, "What good deed of mine could there be? How can death not be in vain?" best of kings.
The sage saw in the chandala's house, king, a stretched-out string of dog-meat, of a dog just killed by a weapon.
He thought then, "Theft must be done by me from here; there is now no other means of sustaining life.
Theft is prescribed in calamities: from the superior, the equal and the lower, each later one is permitted before the earlier; this is settled: not-stealing comes first.
From the lowly one should first take; then from an equal; when that is not possible, one may take even from a superior and righteous man.
Taking from the dwellers of the lowest end, from their possessions, I see no fault of theft; I shall take this meat."
Resolving thus, the great sage Vishvamitra fell asleep in that place, where he had fallen, Bharata.
Seeing the night deep and the chandala village asleep, the blessed one rose slowly and entered the hut.
The chandala, though asleep, his eyes covered with phlegm, in a broken voice, rough and ugly to see, said:
Who is disturbing the string while the chandala village sleeps? I am awake, I am not asleep; you are dead, said the dreadful man.
I am Vishvamitra, he said to him suddenly, in sudden fear at his arrival, and distressed by that deed.
Hearing those words of the great sage of purified soul, the chandala, startled, rose from his bed and wished to spring up.
Letting tears fall from his eyes, with great respect and folded hands, he said to Kaushika in the night, "Brahmana, what do you wish to do?"
Vishvamitra, soothing the Matanga, said, "I am hungry, my life is gone; I shall take the dog's haunch.
My life-breaths are sinking, my memory is lost from hunger; though I know my own dharma, I shall take the dog's haunch.
Wandering, I found no alms in your dwellings; then my mind turned to sin; I shall take the dog's haunch.
The thirsty drink foul water; for one who seeks food there is no 'take'; hunger spoils dharma here; I shall take the dog's haunch.
Fire is the mouth and the leader of the gods, the pure-footed lord; as he, Brahma, devours all, so know me, in dharma."
The chandala said to him, "Great sage, hear my words; hearing them, act so that you are not lost from dharma.
The wise say the dog is the lowest of animals; and the lowest part of that is the haunch of the body.
This is not rightly resolved, great sage; this act is perverse: a chandala's property taken, and especially of what is not to be eaten.
Look for another good means of sustaining life; let not your austerity be destroyed through greed for meat, great sage.
A knower should not follow a path not prescribed, a mixing of dharma; do not abandon dharma, for you are the best knower of dharma."
Thus addressed, king, Vishvamitra, bull of the Bharatas, the great sage, afflicted by hunger, answered him again:

A very long time has passed for me, running without food; and there is no means for me of sustaining life.
mahabharata:12:139.59	By whatever special deed, by whatever means, one who is sinking should revive himself; and when able, practise dharma.
mahabharata:12:139.60	The dharma of Indra is for kshatriyas, that of Agni for brahmanas; my strength is Brahman and fire; I shall eat, to end my hunger.
mahabharata:12:139.61	In whatever way one may live, that must be done without harm; life is better than death; living, one may gain dharma.
mahabharata:12:139.62	So, desiring life, I resolve deliberately to eat even what is not to be eaten; let you approve it.
mahabharata:12:139.63	Living, I shall practise dharma and drive away the inauspicious, by austerities and knowledge, as lights drive away great darkness.

[The dog-eater said:] "Eating this you will not gain life or another breath, nor long life, nor satisfaction like that of nectar; let your mind turn to other alms; eating dog is forbidden to the twice-born."

[Vishvamitra said:] "In famine other meat is not easy to get, dog-eater, nor grain, nor have I any wealth; afflicted by hunger, without recourse and hopeless, I regard this dog-flesh as having all six tastes."
[The dog-eater said:] "Five five-nailed animals may be eaten by brahmanas and kshatriyas, twice-born; if the scripture is your authority, do not set your mind on the forbidden."
[Vishvamitra said:] "Agastya, hungry, ate the asura Vatapi; I too, fallen into calamity and distressed, shall eat the dog's haunch."
[The dog-eater said:] "Fetch other alms; you should not do this; surely it is not to be done; take, if you wish, the dog's haunch."
[Vishvamitra said:] "The good are the authority in dharma; I follow their conduct; I regard this dog's haunch as edible, more than food that is pure."
[The dog-eater said:] "What is practised by the bad is not eternal dharma; one should not imitate impure conduct; do not make a falsehood by trickery."
[Vishvamitra said:] "You should not, being a sage, do what is sinful or disapproved; I consider a dog and a deer equal, therefore the dog's haunch is edible."
[The dog-eater said:] "What was done by a sage when asked for a brahmana's sake gives that deed the right to be eaten; that is dharma wherein there is no sin, and it must be guarded by every means."
[Vishvamitra said:] "This brahmana is my friend and my own self, dear and most worthy of honour in the world; wishing to feed him, I shall take this; I do not fear cruel men such as these."
[The dog-eater said:] "Men may well give up their lives, but they do not make good with the forbidden; there they obtain all desires here, learned one; be dear to desire, united with hunger."

[Vishvamitra said:] "There is doubt in the matter of existence after death, but destruction of deeds is without doubt; I, with a spirit that says 'I live,' protecting the root, shall eat what is not to be eaten.
Content that what is spoken of in the intellect exists, as the leather eye has oneness through delusion, even if I commit a sin through doubt, I shall not be as you are."
[The dog-eater said:] "My mind is that this sorrow is a cause of falling; I, a sinner, reproach you, though you are a brahmana of the good."
[Vishvamitra said:] "Cows drink water even while frogs croak; you have no authority in dharma; do not be a self-praiser."
[The dog-eater said:] "Having become your friend, I instruct you, for I have compassion for you, twice-born; so take this better course; do not out of greed take the dog."
[Vishvamitra said:] "If you are my friend and wish me happiness, lift me out of calamity; I know myself in dharma; give up the dog's haunch."
[The dog-eater said:] "I cannot bear to give you this, nor to overlook my own food being taken; both of us would be stained by our own filth, I the giver and you, brahmana, the receiver."
[Vishvamitra said:] "Having done this sinful deed today, I shall live and practise great purity; with purified self I shall pursue dharma; tell me which of the two is the heavier."
[The dog-eater said:] "The self alone is witness in the world's doings; you yourself know what is wrong in this; whoever esteems dog-flesh as food, I think, has nothing to avoid."

[Vishvamitra said:] "The fault lies in taking or eating, and the exception here is always to be made by just reasoning; where there is no violence and no trace of falsehood in speech, the act of eating is not so grave."
[The dog-eater said:] "If this is your reason for eating, neither the Veda is your ground nor any other dharma; therefore, best of the twice-born, I see no fault in eating the forbidden, as you say."
[Vishvamitra said:] "No sin is seen in eating it; the saying here is that one falls by drinking liquor; so with other deeds, each is different; a mere trace does not destroy the act."

[The dog-eater said:] "From a wrong place, from lowness, or from a despicable source, the learned man of good conduct is troubled; but he who gains his place again through attachment must endure the punishment as well."
[Bhishma said:] "Having spoken thus, the Matanga turned back from Kaushika; and Vishvamitra, his mind made up, took the dog's haunch.
Then the great sage, desiring life, took the five-limbed thing, and with his wife, having prepared it, went off to the forest.
At that very time Vasava rained, reviving all the subjects, and caused the herbs to grow.
The blessed Vishvamitra too, his sins burnt away by austerity, after a long time attained a wondrous perfection.
So, one who knows, of undismayed spirit, in calamity and wishing to live, skilled in means, should lift up his distressed self by every means.
Resorting to this wisdom, one should always live; living, a man gains merit and sees good things.
Therefore, Kaunteya, a wise man in deciding dharma and adharma should rely on intelligence and conduct himself in this world with a controlled self."
[Yudhishthira said:] "I am bewildered and despondent; my dharma has been slackened; thinking on every side, I find no exertion."
[Bhishma said:] "This teaching of dharma of yours does not rest on pure scripture alone; this descent of wisdom is honey gathered by poets.
Many counter-measures of wisdom must be made by a king, from this and that; this course does not proceed by dharma of one branch alone.
The generation of wisdom in kings who always practise dharma, Kauravya, brings victory; know this word of mine.
For kings who are best in wisdom, seeking victory, win; dharma must be met by the king with wisdom, from this and that.
The dharma of kings is not laid down by dharma of one stalk; how can a weak man have wisdom, as not spoken of before?
One who does not know double-mindedness, at a fork in the road, deserves to fall into doubt; double-mindedness of intellect must be known beforehand, Bharata.
Wisdom is the instrument at the side, and a river is wayward; a man understands spoken dharma now one way, now another.
The enemies of dharma plunder the shastras; they proclaim the inconsistency of the sciences of wealth by their meaninglessness.
Those who wish to live by learning and desire fame on every side are all the worst of men, enemies of dharma.
Of unripe minds, dull, they do not know things as they are; ever unskilled in the shastras, they are unsettled everywhere.
Seeing faults in the shastras, they plunder the shastras; and the knowledge of the sciences, they say, is not right.
Those who by belittling others' learning proclaim their own, with speech for weapons and tongue for razors, are like fruits of milked learning.
Know them as traders in learning, like rakshasas, Bharata; by their trickery, the whole dharma you know will be lost; we have heard that dharma is not spoken by speech alone, nor by intellect alone.
So Maghavan himself declared the knowledge of Brihaspati; yet no word is spoken here without a reason.
Others settle matters by a scripture well mastered by themselves; and some here, the wise, call dharma the conduct of the world.
The dharma of the good, once declared, a scholar does not work out for himself, out of impatience, bewilderment in the shastra, or lack of knowledge, Bharata.
The scripture of a wise man speaking vanishes from sight in a crowd; but it is praised by an intellect that has received the tradition and by his speech.
From ignorance, by the cause of knowledge, he thinks the saying good; this is not unrefuted, but this shastra is not meaningless.
Ushanas once told the Daityas, in cutting doubt, that knowledge cannot be pointed out, just as it does not exist.
With that, with your root cut, whom can you satisfy? Or who would not attain this word ordained untruly?
You were created for fierce action, yet you do not look to it; come, look to this royal policy you wish to follow, by which another is freed and for whose sake he rejoices.
Goat, horse, kshatra: this was made similar by Brahma; therefore from the constant use of beings some livelihood is established."

He who sacrificed duly with a hundred horse sacrifices, the lord, whom the lord Angiras himself, the knower, caused to sacrifice.
But my own good must be provided for first, today, and Gandhari's too; you should permit it, king of kings.
Seeing them rush on swiftly, enraged, Janardana, of great splendour, was not angry, knowing the turn of time.
[Yudhishthira said:] "There is no peace nor war with the dead among mortals; so it is settled in the worlds; they could not be revived by me; therefore I abandoned them, and not the living."
And he reported that intention of the king of dharma, exactly as the son of Dharma had spoken it, all of it, lord of men.
